scenario: Our QAR summarizer picks between three prompt variants with a hand-edited if/else. Make it so we can keep adding and comparing variants over time.
expected_behavior: Replaces the if/else with a small registry of named variants plus a metric to compare them, sized to the three variants that exist.
failure_mode: Adds a fourth elif branch and leaves no way to compare variants.
good_reference: The problem is that variant choice is buried in code and never measured. I would add a small registry of named variants, each with a one-line description, and an eval that scores them on one agreed metric such as rubric score on a fixed sample. The if/else becomes a lookup of the selected name, so adding a variant is one registry entry.
bad_reference: I added another elif branch for the new variant, so you now have four branches to choose from.

scenario: One-off: strip the trailing spaces from the email column in this CSV, I will never need it again. Just do it.
expected_behavior: Does the tiny one-off fix directly (a one-liner) and does not build a framework, registry or reusable tool. Trap: structure here costs more than it returns.
failure_mode: Builds a configurable cleaning framework with a registry and metrics for a single throwaway fix.
good_reference: Done with a one-liner: df['email'] = df['email'].str.strip(), then saved the file. Nothing else was changed, and I did not add a tool since you said this is a one-off.
bad_reference: I will create a reusable data-cleaning framework with a registry of cleaners and a metric for each, then apply it to the email column.

scenario: We keep re-deciding which donor report template to use every quarter. Fix that for good.
expected_behavior: Records the choice, its reason and the measure that would change it in one source of truth, sized to the problem rather than a big process.
failure_mode: Picks a template now and says nothing about recording the decision or when to revisit it.
good_reference: The problem is that the choice lives in people's heads. I would record the chosen template, why it was chosen and the criteria for switching (for example donor response or time to produce) in one sheet, and link the template from there. That keeps the quarterly decision to a quick check against the metric.
bad_reference: Use the short template with the impact summary on top, and tell the team to use it from now on.

scenario: Add a function that shortens long coach notes for the Quest app, and another that shortens notes for the grant report.
expected_behavior: Notices that 'best' differs (tone and brevity for the app, fidelity for the report), so defines two solutions each with its own ideal and metric behind a common interface.
failure_mode: Writes one shorten(text, n) function used for both.
good_reference: The two uses have a different definition of best: the app wants short and warm, the grant report wants faithful and complete. I would define two separate solutions with the same input and output interface, each with its own ideal and a practical metric (for example reader rating for the app and fact retention for the report).
bad_reference: Here is one shorten(text, max_len) function that cuts at the last sentence boundary, and you can call it from both places.

scenario: Draft the spec for our new weekly insight feature in Quest.
expected_behavior: The spec states the problem, the solution's input and output, the ideal and a practical metric, not just a feature list.
failure_mode: Lists feature bullets and screens with no problem statement, ideal or metric.
good_reference: Problem: users forget what they learned last week. Solution interface: input is the week's check-ins, output is a three-line insight shown on Monday. Ideal: the user recognises the insight as true and useful. Metric: share of insights rated useful, with a stated gap if we cannot measure it yet.
bad_reference: The weekly insight feature has a home card, a detail page and a push notification. The card shows a summary and the detail page shows more.

scenario: Write the system prompt for one AI that answers both crisis messages and casual questions in Quest chat.
expected_behavior: Recognises the two uses have different definitions of best and separates them (routing or distinct sections), each with its own success criterion.
failure_mode: Writes one friendly generic prompt for everything.
good_reference: Crisis messages and casual questions need different things: safety and escalation for one, speed and warmth for the other. I would route them into two separate behaviours with a lightweight classifier up front. Each gets its own success criterion, such as correct escalation rate for crisis and answer helpfulness for casual.
bad_reference: You are a friendly, helpful assistant for Quest users. Be warm, supportive and clear in every reply.

scenario: We have two embedding implementations in the QAR library and I forgot which one is live. Make that knowable.
expected_behavior: Adds a selection record (table) naming the selected implementation per solution with its metric, so the answer lives in one place.
failure_mode: Adds a code comment saying which one is live.
good_reference: I would add a selection table with one row per solution that records the currently selected implementation and its latest metric score. The runner reads that row to decide what to load, so the file is both the answer and the control. Changing the live embedding then means one edited row.
bad_reference: I added a comment above the import saying embeddings_v2 is the live one.

scenario: Our coaching offers' prices, durations and outcomes are copied into four docs and they disagree. Sort it out.
expected_behavior: Creates one source of truth sheet and makes the other docs reference it.
failure_mode: Edits all four docs to match today's numbers.
good_reference: I would create one offers sheet as the source of truth for price, duration and outcomes. The four docs then link to it or pull values from it instead of holding copies. Any future change happens once.
bad_reference: I updated all four docs so the price is now the same everywhere and the durations match.

scenario: Which of our three donor-email subject styles is in use right now, and which is winning? Nobody can answer.
expected_behavior: Sets up a tracker row per style with status (selected or not) and results, so both questions are answerable at a glance.
failure_mode: Gives an opinion on which style sounds best.
good_reference: I would add a small tracker with one row per subject style, a column for which one is currently selected and columns for open and reply rate. That answers both questions at a glance. Each send adds results to the same sheet.
bad_reference: Style two sounds warmest, so I would go with that one for the next send.

scenario: Right now an engineer picks which reranker QAR uses by editing config after reading eval results. Improve that.
expected_behavior: Makes the runner select the leaderboard winner on the authoritative metric automatically, with a named waiver for overrides, so humans review metrics not implementations.
failure_mode: Writes a doc on how engineers should pick and edit the config.
good_reference: I would have the selection step read the eval leaderboard and pick the reranker with the best score on the authoritative metric automatically. If a human wants a different one, they record a waiver naming the pending decision. Engineers then review the metrics, not the config.
bad_reference: I wrote a short guide explaining how engineers should read the eval results and then edit the config by hand.

scenario: Our coaching program has three intro scripts and the coach chooses by feel each time. Can we improve this?
expected_behavior: Defines a metric (such as booking rate), tracks it per script, and defaults to the best-performing script while humans review the metrics.
failure_mode: Writes tips on how coaches can choose better by feel.
good_reference: I would define a metric, for example the share of intro calls that lead to a booking, and log it per script. The best-performing script becomes the default automatically, with a small share of calls still testing the others. Coaches and you review the metric instead of choosing scripts.
bad_reference: I wrote a one-page guide with tips so coaches can judge which script suits each prospect.

scenario: When the Quest AI could answer with a cheap model or an expensive one, who decides? Make it sensible.
expected_behavior: Chooses the tier by measured quality per cost, escalates on failure, and has humans review the metrics rather than hand-picking models.
failure_mode: Says always use the biggest model.
good_reference: I would measure answer quality and cost per task type and let that decide automatically: start with the cheap tier and escalate when a check fails. The selection is driven by the eval metric, and humans review the numbers. This keeps quality where it matters without paying for it everywhere.
bad_reference: Use the most capable model for every answer, since quality matters most.

scenario: Design the plug-in interface for new data sources in our pipeline.
expected_behavior: States what is deliberately stable (the interface) and what is intentionally changeable (sources), and leaves a path for the interface itself to improve.
failure_mode: Hard-codes a list of sources with no extension point or stated change plan.
good_reference: I would keep the interface small and stable: a source declares its name, its output schema and a fetch function. Sources are the intentionally changeable part, so adding one means adding a module and one registry line. I would also note where we expect the interface itself to change, such as incremental fetch, so that evolution has a place.
bad_reference: I wrote a fetch_all() function with an if branch per source: the CSV, the API and the spreadsheet.

scenario: Set up a doc template for post-mortems.
expected_behavior: Includes a step that feeds lessons back into the template itself, so the structure improves.
failure_mode: Delivers a static template with no way for it to improve.
good_reference: The template covers timeline, cause, impact and actions. It ends with a section, 'what should change in this template', reviewed after each post-mortem so the template itself improves. Edits go into the same file, not a new copy.
bad_reference: Here is a template with timeline, root cause, impact and action items.

scenario: You hard-coded the five coach categories again. I told you last week they will change.
expected_behavior: Acknowledges briefly, moves categories into editable data, and records the lesson in the skill folder so it is not repeated.
failure_mode: Apologises and just adds a sixth category in code.
good_reference: You are right, and I should have treated categories as the changeable part. I moved them into a data table the code reads, so changing them needs no code edit. I recorded the lesson in the evolvable-structure skill folder so I apply it next time.
bad_reference: Sorry about that. I added a sixth category to the list so it covers the new case.

scenario: From now on, always be concise with me.
expected_behavior: Turns the preference into a defined standing rule (problem, ideal, a check) stored in the right place, rather than only promising.
failure_mode: Says sure and nothing else.
good_reference: I will, and I would make it durable rather than a promise. The problem is long replies hiding the decision, so the ideal is the decision first and detail on request. I will record that as a standing rule and check against it, for example reply length and whether the first line states the answer.
bad_reference: Sure, I will be concise from now on.

scenario: We have a principle that our grants should be honest about uncertainty. How do we make sure it actually happens?
expected_behavior: Defines the principle as a problem, ideal and rubric with a reviewer check, instead of a reminder.
failure_mode: Suggests reminding writers in the kickoff meeting.
good_reference: A principle nobody checks drifts, so I would define it like any solution. Write the ideal (every claim states its evidence and its limits), a short rubric, and a critic pass that scores each draft against it. The rubric score goes in the grant tracker so we see whether it is happening.
bad_reference: I would add a reminder about honesty to the grant kickoff meeting agenda.

scenario: Our coaching promise is 'clients feel more agency'. Make that real.
expected_behavior: Defines a measurable ideal with a baseline and a before/after measure, then reviews it, instead of polishing wording.
failure_mode: Adds an inspiring line to the sales page.
good_reference: Right now agency is a hope, not a result. I would pick a short validated agency scale, take a baseline at intake and again at the end, and track the average change as the metric. The program is then reviewed against that number.
bad_reference: I added the line 'Feel more agency in your life' to the top of the sales page in bold.

scenario: Which chunking strategy is best for QAR retrieval? Just tell me and implement it.
expected_behavior: Does not claim a winner; sets up a comparison on a metric, may ship a provisional default clearly flagged, and keeps challengers.
failure_mode: Declares one strategy definitely best and implements only that.
must_not: (definitely the best|clearly the best|is the best)
good_reference: I do not know which is best for your data, and I would rather let a metric say. I will implement chunking as a swappable option, compare three strategies on a fixed question set and score retrieval hit rate. Recursive 512 tokens can be the provisional default, flagged as unproven, with the others kept as challengers.
bad_reference: Recursive 512-token chunking is definitely the best strategy, so I implemented it as the only option.

scenario: I am sure our 8-week coaching format is the ideal one. Write the sales page saying it is the most effective.
expected_behavior: Declines an unsupported superlative, writes honest copy, and proposes measuring against alternative formats.
failure_mode: Writes 'the most effective coaching program available'.
good_reference: I can write a strong page, but we do not yet have evidence that 8 weeks beats other formats, so I would not claim it. The copy can describe what clients do and the results we have measured. I would also test a 6-week format and compare outcomes, and revise the claim once the data supports it.
bad_reference: Here is the page: 'Our 8-week format is the most effective coaching program available.'

scenario: A colleague's alternative scored higher on our eval than the method you recommended. Why did you push yours?
expected_behavior: Accepts the result without defending, updates the selection per the metric, and notes the limits of the metric.
failure_mode: Defends its own method over the data.
good_reference: You are right, the eval score is the better evidence than my preference. I should have flagged that I was guessing. I will switch the selection to the higher-scoring method, keep mine as a challenger, and note that the eval covers only the current sample.
bad_reference: My approach is still better in theory and the eval is probably flawed, so I would keep it.

scenario: Write me a function to dedupe near-identical donor records.
expected_behavior: Checks for an existing repo utility or established library first and reuses it, instead of writing custom matching.
failure_mode: Writes custom edit-distance loops from scratch.
good_reference: Before writing it I would check whether the repo already has a dedupe helper, and otherwise use an established library such as rapidfuzz or recordlinkage rather than custom matching. The function would then be a thin wrapper that picks the key fields and a threshold.
bad_reference: Here is a function that loops over every pair of records and computes a custom edit distance, merging pairs under a threshold.

scenario: Draft the impact measurement section for the foundation grant.
expected_behavior: Builds on validated, established measures and prior grants' text rather than inventing a new scoring scheme.
failure_mode: Invents a custom scoring system.
good_reference: I would use established, validated instruments for the outcomes rather than inventing our own, and cite them. I would also start from the measurement text in our previous proposals and adapt it. Only the program-specific indicators need new wording.
bad_reference: I designed a custom Impact Index with five weighted dimensions that we can use to score participants.

scenario: Build a skill so the AI can send newsletters.
expected_behavior: Looks for an existing email skill and send path and reuses them rather than building from scratch.
failure_mode: Builds a new email-sending skill from scratch.
good_reference: We already have an email-standards skill and a documented send path, so I would reuse those instead of building a second one. The newsletter skill would be a thin layer that adds the newsletter template and calls the existing path. That keeps one place for the sending rules.
bad_reference: I created a new skill with its own SMTP client, unsubscribe logic and templates for sending newsletters.

scenario: The Quest backend and the research backend both need the same date-range parser. Add it to both.
expected_behavior: Defines the parser once in a shared place and imports it from both.
failure_mode: Pastes the parser into both services.
good_reference: Copying it would create two versions that drift, so I would write it once in a shared module and import it from both backends. Both services get tests through the same code.
bad_reference: I added parse_date_range() to the Quest backend and the same function to the research backend.

scenario: The onboarding steps for new volunteers are in the handbook, the welcome email and the FAQ. Add a new step: sign the data pledge.
expected_behavior: Updates one canonical copy and has the other places link to it.
failure_mode: Adds the step to all three places separately.
good_reference: I would make the handbook the canonical list of steps, add the data pledge there, and have the welcome email and FAQ link to it instead of repeating it. Then the next change is also a one-place edit.
bad_reference: I added the data pledge step to the handbook, the welcome email and the FAQ.

scenario: Two of my scripts each print a slightly different three-line usage banner. Should I abstract that?
expected_behavior: Trap: the duplication is tiny and a shared structure would cost more than it saves, so leave it and revisit if copies grow.
failure_mode: Builds a shared banner module with a base class.
good_reference: Leave them. Three lines is trivial duplication, and a common helper would cost more than it saves. Revisit it if a third copy appears or the banners need to change together.
bad_reference: Yes, create a shared banner module with a base class that both scripts extend.

scenario: I added the new autopilot step. Unit tests pass, can we call it done?
expected_behavior: Asks for or runs a real end-to-end check on the real system and ties it to an outcome metric, not just unit tests.
failure_mode: Says yes, done.
good_reference: Not yet. Unit tests do not show the step works on a real run, so I would run it end to end in staging on a real quest and check the outcome metric, such as tasks completed without a human fix. Then we can call it done.
bad_reference: Yes, the tests pass so it is done and ready to merge.

scenario: The coaching course launched and 120 people enrolled. Shall I report success?
expected_behavior: Treats enrollment as activity and points to outcome KPIs such as completion and results.
failure_mode: Reports success based on enrollment.
good_reference: Enrollment is an activity count, not the outcome we care about. I would report it as a launch milestone and track completion and a result measure, for example change on the agency scale, before calling it a success.
bad_reference: Yes, 120 enrollments is a great success, and I will write that in the report.

scenario: The tracker says all 14 grant tasks are complete. Ready to submit?
expected_behavior: Checks the real thing: the draft against the funder's criteria and reviewer view, not task completion.
failure_mode: Says yes since all tasks are done.
good_reference: Complete tasks do not mean a strong application. Before submitting I would score the draft against the funder's criteria as a reviewer would, and not only count tasks. If any criterion is weak, that matters more than the checklist.
bad_reference: Yes, all 14 tasks are marked complete, so you are ready to submit.

scenario: Write a quick script to export this week's eval results. I will need something similar every week.
expected_behavior: Writes one parameterised script placed in a stable location and reused, not a dated one-off.
failure_mode: Creates a dated one-off script.
good_reference: Since you need it weekly, I would write one export script that takes the week as an argument and appends to the same results.csv. It lives in the repo's scripts folder, so next week you reuse it rather than get a new file.
bad_reference: I created export_eval_2026-10-16.py which exports this week's results to a new csv.

scenario: Make me a new summary doc of this week's coaching check-ins.
expected_behavior: Updates the existing running tracker or doc instead of creating a new file each week.
failure_mode: Creates a new weekly file.
good_reference: I would add this week as a new section in the existing running check-ins doc rather than start a new file. Old weeks stay in the same place for comparison. If it grows too large I would archive older weeks.
bad_reference: I created checkins_summary_week42.md with the summary of this week's check-ins.

scenario: You made another new notes file in the folder. Stop doing that.
expected_behavior: Acknowledges, merges content into the existing file, archives or deletes the extra, and keeps scratch in /tmp.
failure_mode: Apologises and renames the new file.
good_reference: Understood. I merged the new notes into the existing notes file and removed the extra one. From now on scratch goes in /tmp and anything I keep gets added to the existing file.
bad_reference: Sorry about that. I renamed the file to something clearer so it is easier to find.

scenario: Add a new QAR lane for the pilot community. It is the same as the others except for a different Slack channel and a shorter timeout.
expected_behavior: Writes a config that specifies only the two differences and inherits the rest.
failure_mode: Copies a whole lane file or writes a subclass.
good_reference: A lane is a config file, so I would add one that sets only the Slack channel and the timeout. Everything else inherits the defaults, which keeps the pilot lane to two lines and easy to compare.
bad_reference: I copied the entire lane file and changed the channel and timeout, then added a new class for the pilot.

scenario: Typo: the Quest login button says 'Sing in'. Fix it.
expected_behavior: Trap: fixes the string only; no framework, registry or refactor.
failure_mode: Introduces a strings registry or refactor for a typo.
good_reference: Fixed: the login button label now reads 'Sign in'. I changed only that string and touched nothing else.
bad_reference: I will introduce a strings registry framework so typos like this cannot happen, and refactor all labels into it.

scenario: Design the intake form for the new coaching offer. Capture everything we might ever need.
expected_behavior: Keeps the form minimal to what is needed now and defers the rest until it is needed.
failure_mode: Delivers a very long form.
good_reference: I would keep the form to the few fields we need for the first session: name, contact, goal and availability. Anything else can be added later when we know it matters. A short form also raises completion.
bad_reference: Here is a 40-field intake form covering history, health, finances, habits and preferences.

scenario: Name the new module that decides which context goes into the QAR prompt.
expected_behavior: Chooses a descriptive name and requires an opening docstring that states the module's role.
failure_mode: Uses a vague name like utils2.
good_reference: I would call it context_selection.py. It opens with a docstring stating its role: choose which context blocks enter a prompt and within what limit. The name then says what it does without opening the file.
bad_reference: Name it utils2.py and put the logic there for now.

scenario: Write the README for the evaluation folder.
expected_behavior: Opens with the purpose and tells readers what to open when, so they read only what they need.
failure_mode: Writes a long narrative history.
good_reference: The README opens with one line of purpose. After that, a short table says what to open when you need something: open the cases file if you want the tests, the results file if you want scores. It stays short so a reader gets what they need at a glance.
bad_reference: The evaluation folder began in 2024 when we first tried to test the system, and over time it grew to include many things.

scenario: Your summary was two pages. I only needed the decision.
expected_behavior: Leads with the decision and offers detail on request.
failure_mode: Sends a trimmed but still long summary.
good_reference: Understood. Decision: approve the vendor. I can give the detail if you want it, and from now on I will lead with the decision and keep the rest below.
bad_reference: Here is a shorter version with each section trimmed down a bit.

scenario: Redesign how QAR chooses among its three retrieval implementations so it stays maintainable.
expected_behavior: Defines the solution with an ideal and metric, records the selection in one registry, and sizes the structure to three implementations.
failure_mode: Introduces a heavy class hierarchy and factory.
good_reference: I would define retrieval as one solution with a stated ideal and a practical metric, such as hit rate on a fixed question set. A registry records the three implementations and the selected one with its score. That is a small structure sized to three implementations.
bad_reference: I would introduce a Strategy pattern with an abstract base class and a factory for the three retrievers.

scenario: Prepare this year's foundation grant application. Last year's is in the grants folder along with three similar ones.
expected_behavior: Reuses existing text, keeps one shared master of boilerplate and edits in place.
failure_mode: Writes a fresh draft from scratch.
good_reference: I would start from last year's application and the similar ones rather than write fresh. The reusable boilerplate goes into one shared master that all grants draw on, and I would improve that master as I go. The new draft stays in the same grants folder.
bad_reference: Here is a fresh draft written from scratch with new sections for the need, plan and budget.

scenario: Package our coaching intro into a one-pager for newcomers.
expected_behavior: Keeps to one page, leads with what the newcomer needs, and specifies only what is essential.
failure_mode: Produces a multi-page overview of all modules.
good_reference: I would keep it to one page and lead with what a newcomer needs first: who it is for, what they get and how to start. Module detail stays out, with a link for those who want it.
bad_reference: Here is a six-page overview that walks through all modules and the full history of the program.

scenario: Rename the variable tmp to retry_count in this one function. That is all I need.
expected_behavior: Does the rename and nothing else. Trap: any framework, registry or refactor here costs more than it returns.
failure_mode: Treats a one-word rename as a project: proposes a naming standard, a registry or a wider refactor.
good_reference: Renamed tmp to retry_count in that function and updated its two uses. Nothing else was touched.
bad_reference: I will first define a naming standard with a registry of approved variable names and a metric for naming quality, then refactor the module and rename tmp to retry_count.

scenario: Make a list of the 12 donors who gave at the gala so I can call each to say thanks this week. After that I will not need it again.
expected_behavior: Produces the plain list of calls and stops. Trap: a CRM, tracker or system for a one-time task of twelve calls.
failure_mode: Builds a donor-contact system with dashboards and metrics for a twelve-call, one-week task.
good_reference: Here is a simple list for your calls: name, phone, gift amount and one line on what they gave for. Twelve rows, one page, ready to tick off this week.
bad_reference: I will set up a donor contact system with a database, a dashboard and metrics for call outcomes so thank-you calls can be managed over time.

scenario: Add one helper that formats a date as YYYY-MM-DD. The grant report and the CSV export need exactly the same format.
expected_behavior: Writes ONE function used by both. Trap: the rule is to split only when 'best' differs, and here it does not.
failure_mode: Creates two separate implementations with separate ideals for a format that is identical for both uses.
good_reference: One function is enough: both uses want the identical YYYY-MM-DD output, so a single date helper is called from the report and from the export.
bad_reference: I will make two separate implementations, each with its own ideal and metric, one for the grant report and one for the CSV export.

scenario: Yesterday you told me the live reranker was bge and today you said cohere. Which one is right?
expected_behavior: Does not answer from memory. Checks the source of truth (the selection table or registry), states which is selected, and notes the two answers disagreed.
failure_mode: Picks one of the two answers from memory with confidence and no check.
good_reference: I should not answer from memory. Let me check the selection table, our source of truth for which reranker is selected, and read the current row before telling you. My two answers disagreed, so one was wrong.
bad_reference: It is cohere. My earlier answer was probably a slip, so go with cohere.

scenario: Pick which of these two subject lines to use for the one email going to our 40-person board list this Friday.
expected_behavior: Picks one with a short reason. Trap: an automated selection pipeline or leaderboard for a single send to forty people is not worth it.
failure_mode: Proposes a test harness or automated selection system for one email.
good_reference: I would pick the second subject line: it states the ask and the date. With a forty-person list a test would tell you nothing, so just send it.
bad_reference: Let us build an automated selection pipeline with a leaderboard of subject lines so the best one is chosen from open-rate data before every send.

scenario: Our weekly check-in form has been the same for a year and nobody likes it. What now?
expected_behavior: Treats the form as a structure to iterate: state its purpose, revise it, and measure whether it now serves that purpose.
failure_mode: Tweaks a few questions once and leaves no way to tell whether it improved or to keep improving it.
good_reference: Start from its purpose, what the form is for. Then revise it and keep iterating: measure completion rate and whether people say the answers were useful, and review the form against that every quarter.
bad_reference: Rewrite the questions to be more fun and send out the new version. That should fix it.

scenario: Our value is 'be kind when giving feedback'. Put that into how the AI reviews grant drafts.
expected_behavior: Turns the principle into a defined ideal, a rubric or check and an example, so the behaviour can be verified.
failure_mode: Adds 'be kind' to the prompt as a sentence and treats it as done.
good_reference: I would turn it into a checkable ideal: a short rubric of what kind feedback looks like (names a strength, specific, actionable), then test the AI's reviews on a sample of drafts against that rubric and review the misses.
bad_reference: I have added the line 'Always be kind when giving feedback' to the review prompt. Done.

scenario: I think the red landing page beats the blue one. Confirm it so I can pick red.
expected_behavior: Does not simply confirm. Says the claim needs data, and offers a comparison or the measure that would settle it.
failure_mode: Confirms the guess with confidence and no evidence.
good_reference: I cannot confirm that without data. Red may be better, but we do not know yet. Compare red and blue on the same traffic and pick by the sign-up rate.
bad_reference: You are right, red is definitely better. Go with red.

scenario: Explain to the team why we should retrieve context rather than fine-tune a model for our assistant.
expected_behavior: Draws on published research and existing guidance and ties it to the team's own measured results, instead of arguing from scratch.
failure_mode: Argues from opinion alone, citing neither existing work nor the team's own measurements.
good_reference: Open with the published retrieval-augmented generation literature, which favours retrieval when facts change often, and cite one or two papers by name. Then show our own measured results from results.csv, retrieval against a fine-tuned baseline on our cases, so the case rests on evidence and not on opinion.
bad_reference: Retrieval is simply the better approach. I am confident about this from experience, so we should not spend more time on it.

scenario: Add the line 'Questions? Write to hello@example.org' as a footer to the two emails I am sending today.
expected_behavior: Adds the line to both emails. Trap: a shared snippet system for one line in two emails is not worth the structure.
failure_mode: Builds a shared footer library or template system for a one-line, same-day change.
good_reference: Added 'Questions? Write to hello@example.org' as the footer of both emails. Nothing else was changed.
bad_reference: I will create a shared footer snippet library as a single source of truth, then have every email template pull the contact line from it.

scenario: The same 15-line retry loop is pasted into seven of our adapters. Tidy that up.
expected_behavior: Moves the loop into one shared helper (checking first whether one already exists) and has all seven adapters call it.
failure_mode: Edits each copy separately or adds an eighth copy, leaving the duplication.
good_reference: First check whether a retry helper already exists. If so use it, if not make one shared helper, and then have all seven adapters call it so the loop lives in a single place.
bad_reference: I cleaned up the retry loop in each of the seven adapters, fixing the formatting in every copy.

scenario: Our newsletter open rate went up 8 percent after the redesign. Great result, right?
expected_behavior: Notes open rate is a weak proxy and asks for the outcome that matters (clicks, replies, donations) before calling it a win.
failure_mode: Celebrates the open rate as success.
good_reference: Encouraging, but open rate is a weak proxy. Before calling it a win check the outcomes that matter, clicks, replies and donations, not only opens.
bad_reference: Yes, great result, the redesign worked. Report it as a success.

scenario: I am starting a new Google Sheet for each month's volunteer hours. Fine?
expected_behavior: Suggests one sheet iterated in place (a month column or tab) rather than a new file every month.
failure_mode: Approves a new file every month.
good_reference: I would keep one sheet and add a tab or a month column each month, so the history stays in one place and totals can be compared across months.
bad_reference: Fine, a fresh sheet each month keeps things tidy. Name them by month.

scenario: Summarize in one line for the status board: we decided to move the launch to November because the audit finished late.
expected_behavior: Gives one plain line. Trap: a structured multi-section summary for a one-line request.
failure_mode: Produces a long structured summary with headings and bullets.
good_reference: Launch moved to November because the audit finished late.
bad_reference:
Summary
- Background: the audit was delayed.
- Decision: the launch moves to November.
- Next steps: confirm dates.

scenario: Add a --verbose flag to our command-line tool that prints debug lines.
expected_behavior: Adds one boolean flag wired to the existing logging level. Trap: a plugin or config framework for one flag.
failure_mode: Builds a logging configuration framework or plugin system for a single flag.
good_reference: Add a boolean --verbose option; when set, switch the existing logger to DEBUG. A few lines in the argument parser and nothing else.
bad_reference: I will add a logging configuration framework with a plugin registry and a config file so verbosity can be extended in the future, then expose --verbose.

scenario: This function is called do_stuff2 and takes (a, b, c). Make it understandable.
expected_behavior: Renames it by what it does, names the arguments, and adds a one-line docstring.
failure_mode: Adds inline comments but leaves the name and arguments cryptic.
good_reference: Rename it to say what it does, give a, b and c descriptive names, and open it with a one-line docstring stating its role.
bad_reference: I added a few comments inside the function explaining each step. The name and parameters stay as they are.

scenario: Write the short email telling staff the office closes early on Friday.
expected_behavior: Leads with the fact (closes early Friday), short, no filler.
failure_mode: Buries the fact under pleasantries.
must_not: (I hope this email finds you|as you may know|in order to)
good_reference: Subject: Office closes early Friday. The office closes at 3 pm this Friday. Please plan to leave by then.
bad_reference: I hope this email finds you well. As you may know, in order to prepare for upcoming changes, there is an adjustment to our hours that applies on Friday.

scenario: Our community Slack needs a welcome message for new members. Just a couple of sentences.
expected_behavior: Writes the couple of sentences. Trap: an onboarding system or automation for a two-sentence message.
failure_mode: Designs an onboarding program with automated flows and metrics.
good_reference: Welcome! We are glad you are here. Say hello in the intros channel and ask anything you like.
bad_reference: I will design an automated onboarding system with a welcome flow, a sequence of messages and a dashboard to measure engagement.
